title: Chalk seas: coccolithophores bloom

facts.text: More chalk formed in the Cretaceous than in any other Phanerozoic period, and the period is named for it.
Chalk is made of coccoliths, the tiny calcite plates of coccolithophore algae that thrived in Cretaceous seas.
Upper Cretaceous chalk forms the white cliffs of Dover and similar cliffs on the Normandy coast of France.
Coccolithophore and other calcareous nannoplankton diversity grew through the Mesozoic, peaking at about 150 species in the Late Cretaceous.

title: Cretaceous seas flood the continents

facts.text: Sea level rose in earnest from the early Cretaceous; by the Cenomanian it stood roughly 250 metres above today's.
At the peak of the Cretaceous transgression, one-third of Earth's present land area lay under the sea.
Other estimates put sea level about 300 metres higher than today, in a hot, humid world with no permanent ice.
Many small, fast-recycled ocean plates made ocean basins shallower, pushing sea levels up.
In North America this flooding, the Zuñi sequence, may have been driven by the Mid-Cretaceous Superplume, and receded late in the period.

title: Gondwana breaks apart into today's continents

facts.text: Gondwana had started to break up in the Jurassic, but its fragmentation sped up in the Cretaceous and was largely finished by the period's end.
Pangaea completed its breakup into the present continents, though they sat in quite different positions.
South America, Antarctica and Australia rifted away from Africa, while India and Madagascar stayed joined; the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans were born.
Gondwana's continental breakup began near Tasmania.
As Pangaea broke up, dinosaurs became strongly differentiated by landmass by the Early Cretaceous.

title: Rudists become the main reef builders

facts.text: Rudists, box-, tube- or ring-shaped bivalves that arose in the Late Jurassic, became major reef builders of the Tethys in the Cretaceous.
Rudist reefs may have driven scleractinian corals out of many tropical shelves, including today's Caribbean and Mediterranean.
They had collapsed by the K–Pg extinction and vanished completely at the close of the Cretaceous.

facts.text: The Cretaceous and its first stage, the Berriasian, begin 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years.
It is the only system boundary still lacking an agreed reference section (GSSP), so its base is formally undefined.
The first appearance of Calpionella alpina, a calpionellid, has been proposed as the marker defining the base of the Cretaceous.
Calpionellids were enigmatic planktonic protists with urn-shaped calcite shells, briefly abundant from the latest Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous.

facts.text: The first dromaeosaurs, the 'raptors', are placed at the start of the Cretaceous.
Teeth possibly from dromaeosaurs are known from the Jurassic, but no body fossils until the Cretaceous.

title: Purbeck Group fauna of southern England

facts.text: The Purbeck Group of southern England spans the latest Jurassic and earliest Cretaceous, and holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Cretaceous faunas.
Its beds formed in a semi-arid setting of freshwater lakes, brackish water, tidal flats and lagoons.
It is famous for fossil insects, with hundreds of species, plus reptiles, early mammals from its 'Mammal Bed', and dinosaur footprints.

title: Carcharodontosaurids spread worldwide

facts.text: Large carcharodontosaurid predators dispersed worldwide in the Early Cretaceous, reaching Africa, North America and South America.
The dispersal may have passed through Apulia in Italy, then joined to Africa by a land bridge, as dinosaur footprints there suggest.

title: Early birds diversify; enantiornithines dominate

facts.text: Avialan birds diversified into a wide variety of forms; some had short, fused pygostyle tails by the Early Cretaceous.
The enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Cretaceous, until they died out with other dinosaur groups at the end of the Mesozoic.
The Jehol Biota holds a great diversity of birds, including the earliest advanced birds; Las Hoyas in Spain preserves many enantiornithines.
Archaic birds had appeared in the Jurassic; true toothless birds arose from toothed ancestors in the Cretaceous.

facts.text: An inland sea, the Eromanga Sea, covered a large part of Australia during the Early Cretaceous.
It was home to the giant pliosaur Kronosaurus.

title: First ants and termites

facts.text: Social termites and ants first appeared in the Early Cretaceous.
Insects diversified during the Cretaceous, when the oldest known ants and termites appeared.
Stem-group ants such as Gerontoformica are preserved in Albian–Cenomanian amber from France.
Many ant groups were present in the Cretaceous, but ants only became dominant, with larger colonies, in the Eocene.

title: First sea turtles

facts.text: The oldest known sea turtles and soft-shelled turtles appeared in the Early Cretaceous.
The first freshwater pelomedusid turtles appeared around 135 Ma.
Turtles became highly diverse in the Cretaceous, as the climate favoured their global dispersal.

facts.text: An asteroid or comet struck central Australia about 142.5 million years ago, very close to the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.
The original crater rim, now eroded away, was about 22 km across; the 5-km ring left today is the eroded central uplift.
Abundant shatter cones are the strongest evidence of its impact origin.

facts.text: A bolide about 2 km wide struck the floor of what is now the Barents Sea off Norway.
It left a 40-km crater, dated to 142.0 ± 2.6 million years ago.
Orb-weaver spiders, builders of wheel-shaped webs, appeared around 140 Ma.

title: North Atlantic rifting splits Europe from North America

facts.text: Europe rifted away from North America between 140 and 120 Ma, in a second major phase of North Atlantic breakup.
The opening seaway let cool water flow from the Boreal Ocean into the Tethys.
The Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift began forming about 140 Ma, a first stage of Greenland's separation.
The Bay of Biscay began opening around 126 Ma and was complete by 85 Ma, uplifting the Armorican Massif.
The new ocean did not follow the old Iapetus suture, stranding Laurentian rocks in north-west Europe and Avalonian rocks in Newfoundland.

sources.title: Opening of the North Atlantic Ocean

facts.text: The Southeast African LIP formed 140–95 Ma at the triple junction where Gondwana split into Antarctica, South America and Africa.
The Mozambique Ridge formed 140–122 Ma, peaking about 120 Ma above the Africa–Antarctica spreading zone.
In a later pulse, 100–94 Ma, the Agulhas Plateau formed with the Northeast Georgia Rise and Maud Rise over the Bouvet hotspot.

title: Eo-Alpine orogeny in the Eastern Alps

facts.text: The Austroalpine nappes of the Eastern Alps were stacked in the first, Eo-Alpine, mountain-building phase, 140–84 Ma.
Africa began moving towards Europe again, and oceanic crust of the Piemont-Liguria Ocean was subducted beneath the Apulian plate.
The first continental collision, of the Adriatic subplate with Europe, came in the Late Cretaceous; the main Alpine mountain building followed in the Paleocene–Eocene.
The Sevier orogeny raised mountains in western North America from 140 to 50 Ma.
It has been tied to North America's collision with a chain of island arcs about 125 Ma; in Utah the Willard thrust sheet moved around 120 Ma.
As its mountains rose in the west, the Western Interior Basin to the east widened.

title: Early Cretaceous cool interval and glacial episodes

facts.text: The cooling of the latest Jurassic continued into the Berriasian, when snowfall was common at high latitudes.
Records suggest glacial periods in the Valanginian, Hauterivian and Aptian, though the Mesozoic was long thought to be ice-free.
Ice-rafted dropstones suggest Northern Hemisphere ice sheets may have reached as far south as Iberia in the Hauterivian and Aptian.
The early Barremian Hauptblatterton Thermal Event marked the final end of the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval.
Deposits laid down directly by glaciers are known only from the Early Cretaceous of the Eromanga Basin in southern Australia.

facts.text: Titanosaurs, the last great sauropod group, lived from about 136 to 66 Ma and were the dominant herbivores of their time.
An early subadult from Paraíba, Brazil, is about 136 million years old.
They spread almost worldwide; titanosaur fossils are known from every continent, Antarctica included.
On the islands of Cretaceous Europe some, like Magyarosaurus, were likely island dwarfs.
The Paraná–Etendeka large igneous province spans the Paraná Basin of South America and the split-off Etendeka traps of Namibia and Angola.
Its lavas covered about 1,000,000 km2 after eruption, with an original volume projected at over 2.3 million km3.
The flood basalts were tied to Gondwana's rifting and the opening of the South Atlantic, over the Tristan hotspot.
Its activity caused the middle Valanginian Weissert Thermal Excursion, a warming event.

facts.text: The Jehol Biota is the ecosystem of north-eastern China between 135 and 121 Ma, preserved in lake beds and volcanic ash of the Yixian and Jiufotang formations.
It holds feathered dinosaurs, including the first known feathered non-avian theropods, many birds, and the largest known Mesozoic mammals.
It also yields the earliest known flowering plants, alongside insects, fish, pterosaurs and amphibians, in huge numbers of individuals.
It has the earliest members of groups that later spread worldwide: neoceratopsians, therizinosaurs, tyrannosaurs and oviraptorids.
Radiometric dating in 2021 placed the Yixian between 125.755 and 124.122 million years ago, a span of about 1.6 million years.
The Weissert Event was a hyperthermal, a rapid global warming in the middle of the otherwise mild Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval.
Carbon dioxide from the Paraná–Etendeka large igneous province is the leading suspected trigger, though its drawn-out eruption leads some to doubt it.
Its carbon-isotope excursion began about 134.5 Ma and its plateau lasted to about 132.4 Ma; estimates of its length run from 1.4 to 2.08 million years.
The warming brought oceanic anoxia but, unlike other anoxic events, no widespread black shales; nannoconid plankton bloomed as ocean productivity soared.
Its end brought sharp cooling, about 1–2 °C in southern France and up to 4 °C around the Boreal Ocean, perhaps even a brief ice age.

facts.text: The earliest widely accepted evidence of flowering plants is single-grooved pollen from the late Valanginian, about 134 Ma, found in Israel and Italy.
Flowering plants appeared in the Early Cretaceous and began to diversify rapidly, a major change of the epoch.
Among the oldest flowering-plant macrofossils are Montsechia from Barremian Spain and Archaefructus (124.6 Ma) from China's Yixian Formation.
Pollen typical of eudicots first appears in the late Barremian, and the earliest monocots are known from the Aptian.
They radiated first in the tropics, then spread toward the poles thanks to the gentle temperature gradient.

facts.text: The middle Hauterivian Faraoni Thermal Excursion followed the Weissert event in a series of Early Cretaceous warmings.
A minor oceanic anoxic event, mostly recorded around the Atlantic, has been proposed for the Hauterivian.

title: Australia begins to separate from Antarctica

facts.text: Separation between Australia and East Antarctica began about 132 Ma; they had begun rifting by 96 Ma, when seafloor spreading between them followed.
The Australian plate was born as it parted from Antarctica and Zealandia, a split finished in the Cenomanian.
By 96 Ma a shallow seaway had begun forming between them, leaving only a narrow link along the South Tasman Rise and Wilkes Land.
A narrow land connection between South America, Antarctica and Australia persisted until about 50 million years ago.
Full separation came much later; the general consensus places it by 60 million years ago.

facts.text: The earliest anglerfish appeared about 130 Ma.

title: South Atlantic Ocean begins to open

facts.text: The South Atlantic started to open about 130 Ma, as the Falkland Plateau, broken from southern Africa at 132 Ma, moved west.
South America began drifting west away from Africa, while Laurasia rotated clockwise and moved north.
Paraná–Etendeka magmatism drove further seafloor spreading c. 135–130 Ma, south of the Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise.
The split also opened the West and Central African Rift System, including the Benue Trough, which began rifting at the start of the Cretaceous.
By the Aptian–Albian, Africa was cut off from the rest of Gondwana and Laurasia, staying an island continent through most of the Cenozoic.

title: India breaks away from Australia and Antarctica

facts.text: The Indian plate broke off from Australia and Antarctica 130–125 Ma, opening the 'South Indian Ocean'.
The Indian Ocean began opening about 130 Ma, its spreading ridge near the Kerguelen hotspot.
Rifts along East Africa, Antarctica and Madagascar formed the southwestern Indian Ocean; India and Madagascar later began to part.
Madagascar stopped moving independently around 120 Ma.

title: North China Craton loses its root

facts.text: Around 130–120 Ma, tectonics in North China switched to extension and its orogenic belts and plateau collapsed, replacing the mantle root.
Retreating Paleo-Pacific subduction may have thinned the craton's lithosphere.
A large igneous province on the Liaodong Peninsula was active c. 131–117 Ma, for 10 million years.

facts.text: Shales and mudstones were laid down in an anoxic, warm, shallow sea that covered much of present-day Colombia.
The IUGS lists it as a geological heritage site for the world's most complete record of Early Cretaceous marine reptiles.

title: High Arctic LIP's first phase opens the Arctic

facts.text: HALIP magmatism lasted from 130 Ma to about 60 Ma; its first, tholeiitic phase ran to 80 Ma with dikes, sills and basalt flows.
It broke up part of the Arctica continent, opened the Arctic Ocean and left radiating dyke swarms.
It still covers over 1,000,000 km2, one of Earth's largest magmatic complexes, though much has eroded away.
Crustal stretching began in the Canadian Arctic Rift System 130 Ma, with widespread sills and dikes intruded 129–127 Ma.
The Iceland hotspot may have started as a plume under the Alpha Ridge c. 130–120 Ma.
An impact left a crater 55–66 km across, now buried deep in the Eromanga Basin of Australia.
Shocked quartz in drill core proved its impact origin; the nearby Talundilly structure may be its twin.

facts.text: Iguanodon bernissartensis, the one well-supported Iguanodon species, lived in Europe about 126–122 million years ago and grew to about 9 m long.
At least 38 individuals were found deep in a coal mine at Bernissart, Belgium, in the Sainte-Barbe Clays Formation.
Once read as a herd that perished together, the Bernissart bones now seem to record at least three separate die-offs, probably from flash floods.
Sinodelphys, from 125-million-year-old shale in Liaoning, China, is the earliest known metatherian, the marsupial line; it had climbing feet.
Eomaia, a eutherian of the same age, shared features with marsupials that the placental line later lost.
Both already had an upright, non-sprawling limb posture.
Other therian mammals are unknown before the Early Cretaceous; the Jurassic Juramaia may itself be Early Cretaceous.
The finds suggest early mammals began to diversify from Asia.
Freshwater wetland limestones at Las Hoyas, Spain, about 125 Ma, preserve dinosaurs and many enantiornithine birds exquisitely.
It yields Montsechia, one of the oldest flowering-plant macrofossils.
In the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution, from around 125 to 80 Ma, flowering plants diversified intensely alongside the pollinating insects that coevolved with them.
Animal-pollinated flowers set off a burst of coevolution: beetles were pollinating by the earliest Late Cretaceous, and moths and butterflies have coevolved with them since.
In the mid-Cretaceous, species diversity on land overtook that of the sea, reversing a pattern held for nearly all of Earth's history.
By 110–90 Ma they dominated forest trees and had displaced conifers, cycads and bennettitaleans by the period's end, though full ecological dominance came only in the early Cenozoic.
Their spread may have sped up weathering and nutrient flow into the oceans, a possible driver of the Mesozoic marine revolution.

facts.text: Heat-driven storms, hurricanes and wildfires plus insect damage made trees produce huge amounts of resin from 125 to 75 Ma.
By the Early Cretaceous, amber formed in concentrations matching or exceeding those of the Carnian.

title: Last temnospondyl amphibians

facts.text: The latest known temnospondyl is Koolasuchus, a chigutisaurid from the Aptian of Australia.
Stereospondyl temnospondyls, including brachyopoids, had survived from the Triassic into the Cretaceous.
All were gone by the Late Cretaceous, leaving lissamphibians (frogs, salamanders and kin) as the only amphibians.

facts.text: Thalattosuchians, marine crocodile relatives abundant in the Jurassic, became scarce and mostly tropical in the Early Cretaceous, their last records in the Aptian.

title: Stegosaurs die out

facts.text: The Early Cretaceous saw seaways expand and sauropods, stegosaurs and other high-browsing groups decline.
The youngest definitive stegosaurs, including Mongolostegus from Mongolia and Yanbeilong from China, date to the Aptian–Albian.
Stegosaurians appear to have died out in the late Early or early Late Cretaceous; reported later finds have mostly proved misidentified.

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field kept normal polarity, with no reversals, for about 37 million years, from the Aptian through the Santonian.
On the calibrated time scale the superchron, chron C34n, began at 120.964 Ma and ended at 83.650 Ma.
Reversals had grown steadily rarer in the run-up to it.
It is one of two well-established superchrons, with the Permian Kiaman.
All Ontong Java Plateau lavas are normally magnetized, so presumably erupted after it began.
The Selli Event, or OAE1a, was a global oceanic anoxic event at the start of the Aptian.
It was tied to large-igneous-province volcanism and killed marine life through warming, ocean acidification and oxygen loss.
Its carbon-isotope shift began within 22,000–47,000 years; the event lasted about 1.1–1.3 million years, and recovery over a million.
Carbon released by Barents Sea intrusions, perhaps 9,000 Gt, may have triggered it.
With OAE2 it was one of the two Cretaceous anoxic events that most changed ocean chemistry, leaving black shales worldwide.

facts.text: Teinolophos, which lived about 120 Ma in Australia, is one of the earliest known monotremes, the egg-laying mammals.
Steropodon, from Australia about 105 Ma, has also been called the oldest monotreme.

title: Last tritylodontids, the final non-mammal cynodonts

facts.text: Herbivorous tritylodontids persisted in Asia into the Barremian–Aptian, at least until around 120 Ma, as Fossiomanus from China shows.
These extremely mammal-like animals were the last surviving non-mammaliaform cynodonts; they died out in the Early Cretaceous.
An impact in what is now Ukraine left a crater 2.7 km wide, dated to 120 ± 10 million years ago.
The crater holds a lens of granite breccia and impact glass under Early Cretaceous sediments.

title: Kerguelen hotspot builds the Kerguelen Plateau

facts.text: The Kerguelen hotspot's output peaked 120–95 Ma, building the Southern and Central Kerguelen Plateau and Broken Ridge.
Kerguelen Plateau and Broken Ridge cover 2,300,000 km2; the province holds about 25 million km3 of lava.
Its earliest products include Australia's Bunbury Basalt (137–130.5 Ma) and India's Rajmahal and Sylhet Traps (118–115 Ma), linked to the eastern Indian Ocean's opening.
Growth of the Southern Kerguelen Plateau 118–119 Ma contributed to oceanic anoxic event 1.
The Kerguelen microcontinent may have carried dense conifer forest in the mid-Cretaceous.

conflicts.note: Flood basalt list, linked to the Aptian extinction (cites 2002)

facts.text: After the Barremian–Aptian Warm Interval, the Aptian–Albian Cold Snap began about 118 Ma.
It ended around 111 Ma with the Paquier/Urbino Thermal Maximum.
Global mean surface temperature fell to about 20.7 °C, and glacial dropstones in western Tethys sediments hint at an ice age.
A minor extinction event struck in the Aptian, around 116 or 117 Ma, seen mostly in marine deposits.
It may be linked to the Rajmahal Traps eruptions in India, from the Kerguelen hotspot.
For plant history it is an important episode, deserving more weight than other minor events.
The Ontong Java, Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus probably formed as one contiguous large igneous province in the south-west Pacific, by far Earth's largest.
When eruptions ended it covered 1% of Earth's surface with 80 million km3 of basalt, several times the Deccan Traps.
The 'Ontong Java event' was the largest volcanic event of the past 200 million years, erupting up to 22 km3 of magma a year for 3 million years.
The Ontong Java Plateau formed around 116 Ma, with a much smaller event around 90 Ma; renewed rifting about 116 Ma split Manihiki from Hikurangi.
Its eruptions were long thought to coincide with OAE1a, but basalt ages of 117–108 Ma and normal magnetization make that unlikely.

title: Pacific Ring of Fire takes shape

facts.text: By about 115 Ma, today's subduction zones had begun to form the Pacific Ring of Fire around South America, North America and Asia.
About 120–115 Ma the Farallon plate was subducting beneath the Americas and north-east Asia, and the Izanagi plate beneath east Asia.
An impact crater in the basalts of southern Brazil, near the Vargeão Dome, has recently been dated to about 115 Ma.
Deinonychus, a dromaeosaurid up to 3.4 m long with a large sickle-shaped claw on each foot, lived in North America about 115–98 million years ago.
Its 1969 description revealed an active, agile predator, launching the 'dinosaur renaissance' and debate over warm-blooded dinosaurs.
Its bird-like forelimbs led Ostrom to revive the idea that birds descend from dinosaurs, which is now almost universally accepted.

title: Oldest grasses

facts.text: The oldest known grass fossils are from the Albian; by the end of the Cretaceous grasses had diversified into modern groups.

facts.text: The Crato and Romualdo formations of north-east Brazil preserve pterosaurs, fish, invertebrates and plants exceptionally well.
The Santana beds lay near the palaeo-equator and are key sites for Early Cretaceous insects.
The Crato Formation was laid down about 113 Ma in a semi-arid lake wetland; limestone nodules formed around carcasses, preserving soft parts and fish stomach contents.
Borealopelta, a 5.5 m nodosaurid ankylosaur, was buried in marine sands and shales of Alberta's Clearwater Formation about 110–112 million years ago.
Washed out to sea after death, it is among the best-preserved dinosaurs of its size, keeping armour, keratin sheaths, skin and stomach contents.
Pigments suggest a reddish-brown, countershaded body; such camouflage implies even this large armoured animal faced predators.
Further oceanic anoxic events, OAE1b, 1c and 1d, struck in the Albian, around 112–100 Ma.
Their black shales lie mostly in the Atlantic region, and some researchers blame local conditions rather than global change.
They fall within one of the longest anoxic intervals in geologic history, about 125–80 Ma, perhaps paced by orbital cycles.
The oldest true snakes are marine simoliophiids such as the Cenomanian Haasiophis from the West Bank, dated 112–94 Ma; timelines of life put snake origins near 90 Ma.
Najash, about 95 Ma, kept a lizard-like skull with some mobile joints of modern snakes; 113-Ma Tetrapodophis, hailed as a snake in 2015, was later placed among lizards.
Snakes evolved from lizards, perhaps burrowers or mosasaur relatives; in the Late Cretaceous they recolonised land and kept diversifying.

facts.text: Temperatures rose sharply after the cold snap ended around 111 Ma, opening the Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse, which lasted until the early Campanian.
A string of Albian hyperthermals followed: Leenhardt (~110 Ma), l'Arboudeyesse, Amadeus (~106 Ma), Event 6 (~102.5 Ma) and Breistroffer (~101 Ma).
Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera show gradual warming from the Albian to peak warmth in the Turonian.
Late Albian tropical seas averaged about 30 °C, while arid belts on land repeatedly pushed north.
In the Cloverly Formation, oxygen isotopes show cool conditions lingering after the cold snap until a late-Albian warming pulse ushered in the hothouse.
Giganotosaurus, a huge carcharodontosaurid that rivalled Tyrannosaurus among the largest predators, lived in Argentina about 111–106 Ma.
A 2026 study re-dated its rock formations from the Cenomanian to the early Albian.
Its South American lineage may have been split from African relatives as Gondwana broke up in the Aptian–Albian.

title: South America and Africa finally part

facts.text: Identical dinosaur footprints in Brazil and Cameroon around 120 Ma suggest a land link survived into the early Aptian.
North of the equator rifting began after 120.4 Ma and lasted until c. 100–96 Ma; the Benue Trough rifted c. 118 Ma.
By 110 Ma the Mid-Atlantic Ridge reached the Proto-Caribbean and South Atlantic, separating South America from Africa and completing the Atlantic's length.
Carcharodontosaurids of South America may have been split from African relatives by this breakup.
Around 100 Ma South Atlantic spreading sped up sharply, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge grew from 1,200 to 7,000 km, and Africa began moving north-east.
Argentinosaurus, from Argentina's Huincul Formation, was among the largest land animals ever, about 30–35 m long and 65–80 tonnes.
A 2026 study placed the Huincul Formation in the Albian, about 106 million years ago; earlier work suggested a younger Cenomanian–Turonian age.
Its close relative Patagotitan, from Patagonia's Cerro Barcino Formation, comes from rocks dated to about 101.62 million years ago.
Patagotitan was first billed as the largest land animal, 37 m and 69 tonnes, but later estimates cut it to about 31 m and 50–60 tonnes.
Titanosaurs were the dominant sauropods of the Cretaceous and include some of the largest land animals known.

title: Polar dinosaurs of Dinosaur Cove, Australia

facts.text: Dinosaur Cove's fossil beds, about 106 million years old, formed on a rift-valley floodplain as Australia began to separate from Antarctica, inside the Antarctic Circle.
Its 'polar dinosaurs' include small plant-eaters such as Leaellynasaura and Atlascopcosaurus; one fossil hints at adaptations to low light during the polar winter.
The poles were seasonally cold, but some dinosaurs lived in the polar forests year-round, under a climate much milder than today's.
As the Farallon Plate subducted beneath North America, rising magma built the plutons of the Sierra Nevada Batholith; most of its granite formed 105–85 million years ago.
Subduction flattened about 80–76 million years ago, shutting down arc magmatism; pluton formation ended around 70 million years ago.
Uplift and erosion later exposed the batholith as the granite peaks of the High Sierra, including Mount Whitney, Half Dome and El Capitan.

facts.text: Burmese amber from Myanmar's Hukawng Valley, 101–99 Ma, has yielded over 1,000 species, mostly insects.
It formed on the Burma terrane, then an island in the Tethys Ocean near the equator, and preserves its small life in exquisite detail; its trade is ethically controversial.
Finds include Chimerarachne, a 100-million-year-old arachnid with silk spinnerets and a tail.

title: Antarctic land bridge links South America and Australia

facts.text: Antarctica linked Australia and South America by land in the Late Cretaceous and early Paleogene.
Marsupials appear to have crossed from South America through Antarctica to Australia then.
Platypus-like monotremes went the other way, reaching southern South America in the latest Cretaceous.

facts.text: Meridiolestidans were the dominant mammals of Late Cretaceous South America, from sabre-toothed Cronopio to herbivorous mesungulatids.
The group lingered until the Miocene in Patagonia.

title: Mesozoic marine revolution peaks

facts.text: Shell-crushing predation, the driver of the Mesozoic marine revolution, was perfected by marine reptiles and other predators in the Late Cretaceous.
Sea urchins radiated into predatory niches and are thought to have perfected coral grazing.
Faster weathering and nutrient flow from the angiosperm boom may have helped drive it.

facts.text: The Mississippi River Delta traces back about 100 Ma, when the Mississippi embayment formed in the Late Cretaceous.

title: Modern birds (Neornithes) originate

facts.text: Modern birds probably arose around the Early–Late Cretaceous boundary, about 100 Ma, and diversified dramatically around the K–Pg extinction.
Most studies put their last common ancestor in the Cretaceous, from Early to latest; a 2015 study placed it at about 95 Ma and the fowl–Neoaves split at 85 Ma.
About 100 Ma the ancestors of all modern birds evolved a more open pelvis for larger eggs; around 95 Ma birds gained a better sense of smell.
A 2024 genomic study put the fowl–Neoaves split near 100.5 Ma, the palaeognath–neognath split around 130 Ma, and later bird orders in step with flowering plants.
Waterfowl (Anseriformes) and shorebirds (Charadriiformes) are the only modern bird orders with an established Late Cretaceous fossil record.

contested_note: Molecular clocks favour a Cretaceous radiation of modern birds while fossils point to a Paleogene one, the 'rocks versus clocks' controversy.

title: Giant theropods of Cenomanian North Africa

facts.text: Mid-Cretaceous North Africa was ruled by abelisauroids, spinosaurids and carcharodontosaurids, found together in the Kem Kem, Bahariya and other beds.
Carcharodontosaurus lived there about 100–94 Ma, and Spinosaurus appears in the fossil record 100–95 Ma.
The region bordered the Tethys as a mangrove coast of vast tidal flats and waterways.
A dramatic shift from arc to rift magmatism around 100 Ma began separating Zealandia from West Antarctica, a split completed about 84 Ma.
Zealandia includes New Zealand, the Campbell Plateau, Chatham Rise, Lord Howe Rise, Norfolk Ridge and New Caledonia.
The Hikurangi Plateau first subducted beneath New Zealand around 100 Ma, during its collision with Gondwana.
The West Antarctic Rift System began stretching in the Late Cretaceous, before Zealandia's Campbell Plateau broke away from Antarctica.

title: Western Interior Seaway divides North America

facts.text: For 34 million years, from about 100 Ma to 66 Ma, the Western Interior Seaway joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean.
It began as an Arctic arm pushing south, the Mowry Sea, which later merged with a southern embayment to complete the seaway.
The seaway split North America into western and eastern landmasses, isolating their plants and animals.
Its bottom waters went through repeated anoxic spells, leaving organic-rich shales that are now a major oil source.
It narrowed late in the Cretaceous into an inland arm of the Gulf of Mexico and vanished in the early Cenozoic.

facts.text: Sauropods vanish from western North America around 98 Ma, in the Cenomanian, starting a gap through most of the Late Cretaceous called the 'sauropod hiatus'.
Proposed causes: competition with ornithischians, habitat lost to the Western Interior Seaway, or sampling bias, though even revised dates leave a mid-Cenomanian to mid-Campanian gap.
It ended shortly before the Cretaceous closed, when Alamosaurus, probably a South American immigrant, arrived; in Europe, trackways and a tooth suggest sauropods persisted throughout.

facts.text: The first true crocodilians (Crocodylia) evolve around 95 million years ago.
Lebanon's Sannine Formation sites at Haqel, Hjoula and al-Nammoura are famous Cenomanian Lagerstätten with exceptionally preserved fossils.
Shrimp, octopus, stingrays and bony fish are common finds; fossil octopuses are among the rarest.

title: Shallow sea splits Africa in two

facts.text: Around 95–90 Ma a seaway linking the Mediterranean and the proto-Atlantic partly flooded the Tuareg Shield; a Cenomanian–Turonian transgression drowned the Kem Kem ecosystem.
Bivalves show a shallow sea split Africa in half in the Coniacian and Santonian, linking the Tethys to the South Atlantic.
The Benue Trough probably formed the main link to the Gulf of Guinea, via the Chad and Iullemmeden basins, where marine Late Cretaceous sediments lie.

conflicts.note: Cretaceous page dates the trans-African seaway to the Coniacian–Santonian

facts.text: By 135–130 Ma Farallon plate subduction had begun along the proto-Caribbean; the Galápagos hotspot started building the province in the eastern Pacific about 95–90 Ma.
Argon–argon dating puts the main magmatism at 95–83 Ma and a second pulse at 81–69 Ma; a plume arriving about 86 Ma spread volcanism into north-west South America.
Volcanism spanned 139–69 Ma, mostly 95–88 Ma, building several oceanic plateaus and hotspot tracks in phases at 124–112, 94–83 (main) and 80–72 Ma.
It holds roughly 4.4 million cubic kilometres of volcanic rock, the Caribbean–Colombian oceanic plateau, whose crust now makes up most of the Caribbean plate.
Its main phase coincides with the Cenomanian–Turonian oceanic anoxic event, suggesting a causal link.

facts.text: The first mosasaurs appear around 94 million years ago.
They went on to rule the Late Cretaceous oceans, filling the role left by the ichthyosaurs.

verification.title: A new lower Turonian mosasaurid from the Western Interior Seaway and the antiquity of the unique basicranial circulation pattern in Plioplatecarpinae

facts.text: Recent work confirms real extinctions of vertebrates, invertebrates and microbes at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition, not just a preservation artifact.
Planktic foraminifera died out in five phases, and trace-fossil diversity plummeted as the event began.
It is one of the lesser extinctions linked to oceanic anoxia, mostly striking marine life.
Warming from the High Arctic and other large igneous provinces is thought to have driven it.
OAE2 is considered the most recent truly global oceanic anoxic event.
Sulfidic, oxygen-free water spread into the sunlit surface ocean, and black shale such as the Livello Bonarelli at Gubbio was laid down.
Osmium isotopes and trace metals point to submarine volcanism from large igneous provinces as a likely trigger.
It left a positive carbon isotope excursion, one of the main carbon isotope events of the Mesozoic.
The interval had the highest carbon dioxide levels of the Cretaceous and was one of the Phanerozoic's hottest.

verification.title: Biotic and Paleoceanographic Changes Across the Late Cretaceous Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 in the Southern High Latitudes (IODP Sites U1513 and U1516, SE Indian Ocean)

facts.text: Warming began at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition and peaked about 90 million years ago, one of the Phanerozoic's hottest intervals.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide rose above 1,000 ppm, against a pre-industrial 280 ppm, with sea level at a highstand.
Tropical seas reached at least 30 °C, perhaps 33–42 °C, and the equator-to-pole temperature gradient was unusually gentle.
Crocodile-like champsosaurs lived in the Canadian Arctic, where mean annual temperatures exceeded 14 °C.
Warmth lasted to the Turonian–Coniacian boundary, broken by brief cool spells; claimed Turonian Antarctic ice is disputed.

conflicts.note: Cretaceous page dates the Cenomanian–Turonian Thermal Maximum to about 94 Ma

facts.text: Ichthyosaurs, present since about 250 Ma, were more diverse in the Cretaceous than once thought, perhaps radiating as continental breakup lengthened the coastlines.
A first extinction pulse at the start of the Cenomanian wiped out two of their three remaining feeding guilds, leaving only unspecialised apex predators.
After the Cenomanian–Turonian anoxic event only Platypterygius hercynicus survived, and it disappeared about 93 million years ago.
Their extinction was a pair of abrupt events, not a long decline, probably tied to the environmental upheaval and climate change of the Cenomanian and Turonian.
Pliosaurs are also reported to have vanished in that anoxic event, and mosasaurs took over the ichthyosaurs' role as rulers of the oceans.

facts.text: Flood basalts erupted across Madagascar between about 92 and 85 million years ago, by argon–argon dating.
Ages run 88–92 million years in the north of the island and 85–88 million years in the south.

title: Andes shift from extension to compression

facts.text: Around 90 Ma the Andean orogeny changed character: faster ocean spreading and stronger subduction turned western South America from extension to compression.
Subducting ocean lithosphere switched from south-east to north-east motion at about the same time.
Back-arc basins in central Chile and Mendoza were inverted, and uplift turned western Peru's marine basins continental, with erosion from the Late Cretaceous onward.

facts.text: The earliest examples of ticks appear around 90 million years ago.
Carcharodontosaurids, the last definitive carnosaur family, became extinct in the Turonian around 90 million years ago.
Carnosaurs had first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, around 174 million years ago.

facts.text: A minor oceanic anoxic event, recorded by organic-rich black shales, has been proposed for the Coniacian–Santonian stages.
Its black shales are more local than those of the major Cretaceous events, found mainly in the Atlantic and nearby areas.

title: Niobrara Chalk forms in the Western Interior Seaway

facts.text: The Niobrara Chalk built up 87–82 million years ago from the coccoliths of microorganisms in the Western Interior Seaway; it underlies much of the Great Plains.
Its Smoky Hill Chalk is famous for rich marine fossils, including plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, pterosaurs and primitive aquatic birds.
Pteranodon, a pterosaur with wingspans over 6 m, occurs in most of its layers; about 1,200 Pteranodon specimens are known.
Maiasaura, a duck-billed dinosaur, lived in what is now Montana and Alberta about 86.3 to 70.6 million years ago.
It raised its young in colonies of closely packed earthen nests, about 7 m apart, each holding 30 to 40 eggs.
Hatchlings with weak legs and worn teeth show adults brought food to the nest, the first evidence of parental care in dinosaurs.
The first hadrosaurids appear around 86 million years ago.
An impact in the Santonian made the Praia Grande crater, about 20 km across, in Brazil's Santos Basin.
The crater is well preserved, buried beneath 4 km of younger rock.

title: Late Cretaceous cooling begins

facts.text: From the Santonian, near the end of the mid-Cretaceous hothouse, global climate began to cool, a trend continuing through the Campanian.
Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera show peak warmth in the Turonian, followed by gradual surface cooling to the end of the Maastrichtian.
Tropical sea surfaces cooled from about 35 °C in the early Campanian to about 28 °C in the Maastrichtian; turtles declined during a Campanian cooling event.
The Late Cretaceous stayed warmer than today, but its cooling trend, including a Campanian–Maastrichtian cool, dry phase, continued into the Cenozoic.
Whether continental ice sheets existed is unclear, given conflicting ocean-temperature estimates.

title: Zealandia splits from Australia, opening the Tasman Sea

facts.text: The continent of Zealandia, stretching from New Caledonia to New Zealand's subantarctic islands, separated from Australia about 85 million years ago.
About 83 million years ago a rift entering eastern Tasmania split the Lord Howe Rise from the South Tasman Rise.
The Lord Howe Rise, a 3,000 km continental ribbon, drifted off as rifting opened the Tasman Sea and new crust formed in the deep Tasman Basin.

title: Second phase of the High Arctic LIP

facts.text: The High Arctic Large Igneous Province entered a second phase about 85 million years ago, erupting mildly alkaline flood basalts until about 60 million years ago.
The province as a whole was active from about 130 to 60 million years ago.
Earth's magnetic field ended the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (C34n), a 37-million-year stretch with no polarity reversals.
Calibrated ages place the superchron from 120.964 Ma to the start of chron C33r at 83.650 Ma.
Since the superchron, the frequency of reversals has generally increased slowly.

facts.text: India rifted from Madagascar about 83 Ma and drifted rapidly north toward Eurasia, reaching about 18 cm per year in the Paleocene.
The Indian plate's very rapid northward drift, covering about 6,000 km, began around 84 million years ago.
By about 83.5 million years ago seafloor was spreading between India and Antarctica, asymmetrically near the Kerguelen Plateau.
Late Cretaceous flood basalts up to 200 m thick spread over Madagascar.

title: Seafloor spreading opens the northern North Atlantic

facts.text: By about 83 million years ago seafloor spreading had begun in the North Atlantic between the Rockall Basin and North America.
The Atlantic began opening between Ireland and Greenland after 85 million years ago.
Rifting among the Eurasian, Greenland and North American plates may have begun around 81 million years ago.

facts.text: From about 83 million years ago Iberia converged with Europe, until it stopped moving relative to Europe 67.7 million years ago.
In the Pyrenees, compression had replaced extension by the early Turonian, about 90 million years ago.
The Bay of Biscay finished opening into ocean by about 84 million years ago.

title: Kerguelen hotspot builds the Ninety East Ridge

facts.text: The Kerguelen hotspot built the 5,000 km Ninety East Ridge between 82 and 38 million years ago, at or near a spreading ridge.
The oldest dated volcano of the Hawaiian hotspot chain, at its northern end, is 81 million years old.
The Emperor seamounts, the chain's oldest and most eroded part, are 39 to 85 million years old.
The first palm trees appear around 80 million years ago.
A small impact made the 3.5 km Zeleny Gai crater in Ukraine, dated only loosely to 80 ± 20 million years ago.
Mountain building began in western North America in the Late Cretaceous, 80 to 70 million years ago.
It unfolded as buoyant terranes were accreted during subduction of the Farallon plate.
The orogeny raised the Rocky Mountains and started uplifting the Grand Canyon region around 75 million years ago.

facts.text: An asteroid about 1.6 km across struck about 77.85 million years ago, in the Campanian.
It left a crater about 22–23 km wide and 750 m deep, now Lake Lappajärvi, one of Finland's largest.
Rivers draining to the Western Interior Seaway laid down Alberta's Dinosaur Park Formation about 76.5–74.8 million years ago, burying many articulated dinosaur skeletons.
Dinosaur Provincial Park is one of the world's richest dinosaur fossil sites, with 58 dinosaur species among nearly 500 species of fossil life.
Coastal plains hosting such diverse communities were later lost as the Late Cretaceous seas retreated.
Velociraptor first appears around 75 million years ago.
In Mongolia's Djadokhta Formation, a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops were buried locked in combat 75–71 million years ago.
The pair gives direct evidence of predatory or aggressive behaviour among non-avian dinosaurs.
How they were buried is debated; proposals include drowning, a collapsing dune and a sandstorm.
An asteroid or comet nucleus struck near present-day Manson, Iowa, about 74 million years ago.
It left a buried impact structure about 35 km across.

title: Atlantic floods Patagonia

facts.text: A transgression from the Atlantic laid down the marine Jagüel and Roca formations in Patagonia, from the Maastrichtian into the Danian.
Subsiding foreland basins east of the early Andes let Atlantic waters reach the mountain front in the Maastrichtian.

title: Bennettitales die out

facts.text: Bennettitales (cycadeoids), seed plants present since the Permian, were widespread in the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous but declined severely in the Late Cretaceous as flowering plants rose.
They died out in most areas toward the end of the Cretaceous, with the last northern records in polar latitudes.

facts.text: Sea level fell in the final stage of the Cretaceous by more than at any other time in the Mesozoic.
This Maastrichtian regression is one of the proposed contributors to the K–Pg extinction.

facts.text: About 70.5 million years ago surface and bottom waters cooled sharply, and marine species richness rose by 43%.
Cooling peaked about 67.5 million years ago, with surface waters at 13 °C, as richness and productivity began to fall.
The Western Interior Seaway was coldest in the early Maastrichtian, about 16 °C, warming to about 22 °C later.
Carbon was increasingly stored in the deep sea from the mid-Maastrichtian, possibly through cooling and stronger deep circulation.
Ice sheets and sea ice appear to have briefly returned to Antarctica near the very end of the Maastrichtian.
The mosasaur Mosasaurus evolves around 70 million years ago.
In the Maastrichtian, several large mosasaurs shared and competed in the Tethys Sea.
Multituberculate mammals increased in diversity around 70 million years ago.
In the Late Cretaceous they radiated as herbivores and into forms like squirrel-like tree dwellers, peaking in diversity.
The Labrador Sea started opening 69 million years ago, in the Maastrichtian.
Seafloor spreading in the southern Labrador Sea moved Greenland north relative to North America.

title: Modern bird lineages before the extinction

facts.text: Vegavis, from the Maastrichtian, shows that modern birds had begun diversifying before the Cenozoic.
Asteriornis, also Maastrichtian, appears close to Galloanserae, the earliest-branching neognath lineage.
A Vegavis specimen dated 69–66 million years ago holds the oldest known syrinx, the bird voice organ.

facts.text: Quetzalcoatlus, one of the largest flying animals ever, first appears around 68 million years ago.
Tyrannosaurus, the largest land predator of western North America, appears in the fossil record 68–66 million years ago.
The first species of Triceratops appears at the same time.
Ankylosaurus, living 68–66 million years ago, was among the last non-avian dinosaurs.

title: Hell Creek and Lancian dinosaur faunas

facts.text: Montana's Hell Creek Formation records rivers, deltas and swamps on the low eastern coast facing the Western Interior Seaway.
It yields Tyrannosaurus and Ankylosaurus and is a key record of dinosaurs right up to the K–Pg boundary.
This Lancian fauna is closer to East Asian and Canadian–Alaskan faunas than most earlier North American ones.

title: Deccan Traps erupt in India

facts.text: The Deccan Traps began erupting in western India 66.25 million years ago, fed largely by the Réunion hotspot; the bulk erupted 66–65 million years ago.
Eruptions came in three phases, two before the K–Pg boundary and one after, leaving about 1.5 million cubic kilometres of lava.
They warmed climate about 3 °C over the last 100,000 years of the Cretaceous, with a brief 5 °C cold snap 30,000 years before the boundary.
Plant fossils record a 250 ppm rise in carbon dioxide across the boundary, likely from Deccan activity.
Once proposed as a major extinction cause, they are now generally held to have played a minor role at most.

contested_note: Its role in the K–Pg extinction is disputed: the Deccan Traps page calls a minor role at most generally accepted, while the K–Pg boundary page keeps a joint-cause view.

facts.text: An asteroid about 10 km wide struck just off the Yucatán Peninsula, leaving the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across.
Its date matches the K–Pg boundary; 2013 argon dating gave 66.043 ± 0.043 Ma, and impact glass matches boundary ash.
It spread an iridium-rich clay with shocked quartz and tektite glass worldwide, and megatsunamis swept the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean.
A lingering impact winter halted photosynthesis, and the oceans rapidly acidified.
It is widely accepted as the primary cause of the K–Pg extinction, the only mass extinction definitively tied to an impact.

facts.text: About 76% of species and 47% of genera vanished, including all non-avian dinosaurs, in the fifth and latest great mass extinction.
On land every animal over 25 kg died, along with all pterosaurs and many mammals, birds, lizards, insects and plants.
At sea it killed plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, ammonites and rudists, over 90% of coccolithophore species and about 60% of reef-coral genera.
It was rapid, perhaps under 10,000 years, and ocean productivity and circulation collapsed for at least tens of thousands of years.
All major mammal lineages and most turtles survived; mammals then expanded into the large-animal niches dinosaurs left.

facts.text: Ammonoids, present since about 410 million years ago, vanished during or soon after the K–Pg extinction.
Their planktonic eggs and larvae were devastated; of all cephalopods, only nautiloids and coleoids survived.
A few ammonite genera, such as Baculites and Hoploscaphites, may have lingered briefly into the earliest Danian.
Belemnites, already declining and confined to a few high-latitude regions, died out in the K–Pg extinction.
As with ammonites, their embryos probably could not survive ocean acidification; sea butterflies replaced their larvae in the food chain.
Azhdarchid and nyctosaurid pterosaurs were present in the Maastrichtian and likely died out at the K–Pg boundary.
All pterosaurs perished in the K–Pg extinction.
A bone bed in New Jersey's Hornerstown Formation, the Main Fossiliferous Layer, is one of the few sites recording mass death at the K–Pg boundary.
Iridium and shocked quartz in the layer suggest it formed from ecosystem collapse during the extinction.
The 66-million-year-old layer is rich in marine life from the shallow sea that covered southern New Jersey.
Scientists agree that all non-avian dinosaurs, then an estimated 628 to 1,078 species, died out at the K–Pg boundary.
Found in Maastrichtian rocks on every continent, they are absent from Cenozoic rocks everywhere; birds are the only surviving dinosaur lineage.
Their large size, few small species and no known ability to burrow, swim or dive may have left them exposed.
Whether they were already declining is uncertain; 2025 dates on New Mexico beds show diverse faunas into the latest Maastrichtian.
Titanosaurs, the last long-necked sauropods, were still thriving when the extinction struck.

title: Proposed Shiva impact structure

facts.text: The potential Shiva crater, 450–600 km across, would far exceed Chicxulub and has been dated to about 66 million years ago.
Sankar Chatterjee and colleagues proposed it formed at the K–Pg boundary and helped cause the extinction.

contested_note: Shiva is only a proposed, unconfirmed impact structure.

facts.text: Reef-building rudist clams and giant inoceramid bivalves died out at the K–Pg boundary; most inoceramids had been declining well before.
Rudists were once thought to have died out half a million years early, but apparently fell to the K–Pg event itself.
Inoceramids, a bivalve family known from the Permian to the latest Cretaceous, included giants: Inoceramus shells exceeded 1 m, and one Greenland specimen reached 1.87 m.
At Tanis, North Dakota, seismic waves from the impact 3,000 km away raised 10–100 m seiche waves in the Western Interior Seaway within minutes.
The waves flung marine, freshwater and land animals and plants inland while microtektites from Yucatán rained down.
Its fossil fish suggest the impact struck in Northern Hemisphere spring.
